title: The Books: how the magical alphabets passed from hand to hand
summary: The magical alphabets reached the modern world through a short chain of books. Trithemius's Polygraphia (July 1518) printed the Theban, which he ascribes to Honorius of Thebes; Abraham de Balmes's Hebrew grammar (Venice, 1523) printed the first ring-letter alphabet in Europe; and Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (July 1533) gathered the Theban and three Hebrew-keyed alphabets into a working handbook, whose woodcuts reached the modern charts through the English of 1651 and Barrett's Magus (1801). Beside that chain ran the compendia of the world's alphabets (Postel 1538, Ambrosius 1539, Vigenère 1586, Duret 1613, Kircher 1652–79), which set the magical alphabets beside real scripts, and the revival of Lévi, Paul Christian and the Golden Dawn (1854–1888 and after), which put them back to use.

Behind both stand manuscripts: the charaktêres of ancient magic, the medieval Jewish ring-letter alphabets, and Agrippa's draft of 1509–10, whose contents regarding the alphabets are not established.

claims.claim: Honorius of Thebes devised the Theban alphabet.
claims.evidence: Trithemius (1518) ascribes it to 'Honorius surnamed the Theban' on the testimony of Pietro d'Abano's 'greater fourth book'. No such book of d'Abano is known, the alphabet is not in the Liber iuratus, and no copy earlier than 1518 is known. Write: 'Trithemius ascribes it to Honorius of Thebes'.
sources: Peterson, introduction to The Sworn Book of Honorius

claims.claim: Agrippa took the Theban from Trithemius.
claims.evidence: Agrippa III.29 repeats the ascription to Honorius through 'Petrus Apponus', fifteen years after the Polygraphia, and Peterson's edition annotates the chapter with the Polygraphia passage. Agrippa does not name Trithemius at this point; the dependence rests on the agreement of the texts and on the documented contact of 1509–10.

claims.claim: Agrippa invented the Celestial, the Malachim and the Passing of the River.
claims.evidence: Against: Agrippa presents them as writings found among the Hebrews, 'delivered by Cabalists'; the River script was printed by de Balmes (1523) and Panteo (1530) before him; ring-letter alphabets keyed to Hebrew stand in medieval Jewish manuscripts (Bohak 2011; Macfarlane 2025). His book is the main route by which they reached later readers, which is why his name is attached to them.

claims.claim: De Balmes's grammar (Venice, 1523) printed the first ring-letter alphabet in Europe.
claims.evidence: Macfarlane (2025): 'the first Brillenbuchstaben alphabet to be printed in Europe'. Peterson and Wikipedia give sig. B6v.

claims.claim: The River script is the writing Abraham used when he crossed the Euphrates.
claims.evidence: Panteo (1530) is the first known to assign it to Abraham (Macfarlane, following Campanini). Blavatsky (1892) offers another river, the Chebar of Ezekiel. The Hebrew name ever ha-nahar, 'beyond the River', has a Talmudic background that Christian readers did not know (Campanini).

claims.claim: The Celestial alphabet is read from the stars.
claims.evidence: Agrippa gives a one-line etymology: it is called celestial 'because they shew it placed and figured amongst the Stars'. Postel (1538, per a bookseller's description) and Gaffarel (1629) built star-letter theories; Macfarlane (2025) gives the history. No source found shows that any Celestial letter matches a constellation.

claims.claim: Agrippa's 1510 draft already contained the alphabets.
claims.evidence: Not established either way. The draft exists (Würzburg UB, M. ch. q. 50) and is printed in Perrone Compagni's edition (1992), which was not consulted. The '1510' date sometimes given for the Malachim comes from the draft, not from any sight of the alphabet in it.

claims.claim: The alphabets of Adam, Enoch, Abraham and Moses printed by the compilers are the scripts of the patriarchs.
claims.evidence: [P] Rocca (1591), de Bry (1596) and Duret (1613) print alphabets under these names, as I recall. They record what was believed about the invention of writing. Not verified in this run.

claims.claim: Theseus Ambrosius printed characters written by a demon at the conjuring of Ludovicus Spoletanus.
claims.evidence: [P] As I recall, Ambrogio reports the story and prints the characters (1539); later compilers copy them. Not verified in this run; low confidence.

claims.claim: Duret took his magical alphabets from Agrippa, Ambrosius and Vigenère.
claims.evidence: [P] As I recall, Duret names his sources as he goes. Not verified in this run; check the 1613 scan.

claims.claim: The Enochian alphabet was given by angels.
claims.evidence: Dee records it as shown in Kelley's visions, and wrote out his table on 6 May 1583 (Sloane MS 3188, f. 104). Report it as Dee's record.

claims.claim: The Shawq al-mustahām is by Ibn Waḥshiyya.
claims.evidence: Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts the ascription.

claims.evidence: A working hypothesis only: its usual values match Christian's arcana. Not checked against the 1870 book; earlier candidates (Christian 1863; the Paracelsian editions; Duret 1613) are not excluded.

letters.name: The charaktêres of the Greek magical papyri, curse tablets and gems
letters.value: No alphabet: rows of ring-ended signs (charaktêres) that stand for no letter
letters.translit: Papyri, lead, metal and stone; no single book
letters.form: The prelude, not a book. The Greek magical papyri, the lead curse tablets, the metal lamellae and the engraved gems of the Roman period set rows of signs, many with small rings at the ends of their strokes, beside divine names and voces magicae, to be copied exactly as given. They are not letters and spell nothing. Their line runs on into Jewish amulets of Late Antiquity, Coptic ritual handbooks and the recipe books of the Cairo Genizah, and from there into the medieval ring-letter alphabets keyed to Hebrew (Bohak 2011). Standard edition of the papyri: K. Preisendanz, Papyri Graecae Magicae (1928–31; 2nd ed. A. Henrichs, 1973–74).
letters.note: [S] charakteres.json. That file's own basis for the ancient material is mostly prior knowledge; the Bohak 2011 article is search-backed. Show this as the opening card of the lineage, marked as signs, not an alphabet.
letters.author: anonymous practitioners and scribes
letters.date: c. 1st–5th century CE; most of the material 2nd–5th century
letters.place: Egypt for the papyri; the lead tablets, lamellae and gems come from across the Roman world
letters.tookFrom: Not known.
letters.gaveTo: Late Antique Jewish amulets; Coptic handbooks; Genizah recipe books; ultimately the ring-letter alphabets.
letters.dating: Conventional period dating of the corpus; no single object is dated here.

letters.name: Shawq al-mustahām, ascribed to Ibn Waḥshiyya
letters.value: A catalogue of 'ancient', planetary and sages' alphabets, many drawn with ring-ends
letters.form: An Arabic book of the scripts of the ancients. It presents a series of alphabets as the writing of earlier peoples, of the planets and of the sages, many of them drawn with ring-ends, and it has a section on Egyptian hieroglyphs. It survives in manuscript, and its tables were re-copied and varied like other collections of the 'pens' (aqlām) of the sages. It reached European print only in 1806, in Joseph Hammer's London edition with an English version. No link between it and the Hebrew-keyed alphabets of Agrippa is documented.
letters.note: [S] ibn-wahshiyya.json. That file also had no web search and gives no URLs. Keep the ascription as an ascription, and do not say the book deciphered the hieroglyphs.

letters.date: If the ascription holds, about 900–930 CE: his Nabatean Agriculture was dictated in 318 AH / 930–31 CE, according to its transmitter. The date of the earliest surviving manuscript of the Shawq is not established.

letters.gaveTo: Hammer's edition (London, 1806); Okasha El Daly's re-reading of its hieroglyph section (2005).
letters.dating: Depends on the ascription, which Hämeen-Anttila (2006) doubts.

letters.name: Medieval Jewish magical and kabbalistic manuscripts: the ring-letter alphabets
letters.value: Alphabets of ring-letters (Brillenbuchstaben) keyed one-for-one to the 22 Hebrew letters, as writings of angels
letters.form: In medieval Jewish manuscripts the old signs were set against the Hebrew alphabet: each of the 22 letters was given a ring-ended counterpart, and the whole was treated as the writing of angels. Bohak (2011) follows the signs from Greek into Jewish magic and down to these alphabets. Macfarlane (2025) shows how learned Christians took such Brillenbuchstaben from kabbalistic manuscripts and came to treat them as alphabets derived from the stars and authored by angels. Later Jewish charm books still carry them, for instance British Library Or 10161, fol. 21v.
letters.note: [S] charakteres, celestial, malachim, transitus-fluvii (Macfarlane 2025, abstract and snippets; Bohak 2011; Rylands blog, 2022).
letters.author: anonymous Jewish practitioners and scribes
letters.date: Medieval. The Genizah material runs from about the 10th to the 13th century and later; the kabbalistic manuscripts are later still. No single dated manuscript with such an alphabet is named in this research.
letters.place: The Cairo Genizah; Jewish communities of the Mediterranean and of Europe
printed: Hebrew-keyed ring-letter alphabets (names and number vary)
letters.tookFrom: The charaktêres of Graeco-Egyptian and Late Antique Jewish magic (Bohak 2011).
letters.gaveTo: Abraham de Balmes's printed 'script beyond the River' (1523); the three Hebrew-keyed alphabets of Agrippa III.30 (1533), by a route that is not documented.
letters.dating: Period only. Do not date any one of the printed alphabets to a medieval manuscript without a shelfmark.

letters.name: Agrippa's first draft of De occulta philosophia, sent to Trithemius
letters.value: Not established whether it holds any of the alphabets
letters.form: Agrippa visited Trithemius at Würzburg and afterwards sent him a draft of his book on occult philosophy, with a dedicatory letter. Trithemius answered on 8 April 1510, praising it and advising him to share such things only with fit friends. The draft survives at Würzburg. Whether it already holds the Theban of III.29 or the three Hebrew-keyed alphabets of III.30 has not been established here. Vittoria Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Leiden: Brill, 1992) prints the draft beside the text of 1533 and would settle the question.
letters.note: [S] malachim, celestial, trithemius (Stanford Encyclopedia for the draft and the reply; the shelfmark from the sibling files). [H] house timeline for the visit and the reply. Do not call Agrippa Trithemius's pupil: the documented contact is the visit and the letters.

letters.date: 1509–1510. Trithemius dated his letter of reply 8 April 1510.
letters.place: Written after Agrippa's visit to Trithemius at the abbey of St Jakob, Würzburg. The manuscript is now Würzburg, Universitätsbibliothek, M. ch. q. 50.
letters.tookFrom: If the alphabets are there, Trithemius is the obvious source; this is not documented.
letters.gaveTo: The printings of 1531 (Book I) and 1533 (all three books).
letters.dating: The manuscript and the date of the reply are solid. A '1510' date given for the Malachim (Wikipedia's infobox) belongs to this draft and is not evidence for the alphabet.

letters.name: Trithemius, Polygraphiae libri sex
letters.value: Theban, set on the Latin order A–Z and ending in a sign labelled 'w'; other alphabets in the same catalogue
letters.translit: [Basel or Oppenheim]: at the expense of Johannes Haselberg, July 1518
letters.form: The first printed book of cryptography, and the earliest printed home of a magical alphabet that this research can document. Among its illustrated alphabets is one introduced as 'another alphabet, of Honorius surnamed the Theban', by which he hid his 'follies in magic', as Petrus de Apono (Pietro d'Abano) testifies 'in his greater fourth book'. No copy of this alphabet earlier than 1518 is known. No such passage has been found in the writings attributed to d'Abano, and the alphabet is not in the Liber iuratus Honorii. Agrippa reprinted it fifteen years later.
letters.note: [S] theban, trithemius (Library of Congress, Folger, UVaDoc, Wellcome and Met records; Peterson; Wikipedia).
letters.native: Polygraphiae libri sex Ioannis Trithemii abbatis Peapolitani, quondam Spanheimensis, ad Maximilianum Caesarem
letters.author: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), abbot of Sponheim, then of St Jakob at Würzburg
letters.date: Written at Würzburg about 1508 (the Library of Congress says it was begun in 1508; German Wikipedia says it was finished then). Printed after the author's death: the colophon reads '1518 mense Iulio'.
letters.place: Basel or Oppenheim; the sources disagree. The colophon names the bookseller Johannes Haselberg 'de Aia', who paid for the printing. The Folger catalogue gives the printing chiefly to Michael Furter of Basel; other repertories name Adam Petri (Basel) or Jacob Köbel (Oppenheim). The Metropolitan Museum credits the woodcuts to Hans Springinklee.

letters.tookFrom: For the Theban, Trithemius names Pietro d'Abano's 'greater fourth book'; no such book is known. Report this as Trithemius's ascription.
letters.gaveTo: Agrippa, III.29 (1533); the French Polygraphie (1561); the cipher alphabet of the Golden Dawn Cipher Manuscripts (1887), which is taken from Trithemius.
letters.dating: Do not date the printing to 1508: say 'written about 1508, printed July 1518'.

letters.name: Abraham de Balmes, Mikneh Avram (Peculium Abrae)
letters.value: Transitus fluvii: Ketav ever ha-nahar, 'script beyond the River'
letters.form: A Hebrew grammar with a Latin version, printed by Daniel Bomberg. Among the scripts it shows as derived from the 'Ashuri' square letter is one of ring-letters, Ketav ever ha-nahar, 'script beyond the River', labelled in Latin 'scriptura transitus fluuii'. Macfarlane (2025) calls it the first Brillenbuchstaben alphabet printed in Europe. It stands in a grammar, not in a book of magic. Campanini (2014) argues that its terse Latin label, whose Talmudic background Christian readers did not know, set off the later misreadings.

letters.name: Giovanni Agostino Panteo, Voarchadumia contra alchimiam
letters.value: The River script, assigned to Abraham; an 'Enochian' alphabet, assigned to Enoch
letters.form: An alchemical treatise that sets out three sacred scripts in a bilingual Hebrew–Latin passage: Hebrew for Moses, an 'Enochian' alphabet for Enoch, and, under the heading 'Haec est scriptura transitus fluuii', the River script for Abraham. Macfarlane, following Campanini, makes Panteo the first of many to read it as the script Abraham used when he crossed the Euphrates. Panteo's 'Enochian' is not the alphabet John Dee recorded in 1583.

A blog post (Pelling, Cipher Mysteries, 2009) reports a claim that Panteo's alphabet is 'a conglomeration of all three of Agrippa's alphabets'. If that is so, Malachim-like signs were in print three years before Agrippa. It is second-hand and unchecked.

letters.name: Agrippa, De occulta philosophia libri tres
letters.value: Theban (III.29); Celestial, Malachim and Transitus fluvii in one woodcut (III.30); the nine chambers (III.30); the planetary squares, seals and characters (II.22); the geomantic characters (II.51)
letters.form: The book through which nearly every later reader met the magical alphabets. Book III, chapter 29 ('Of the Characters and Seals of Spirits', in the English of 1651) sets the Theban among the secret characters, as letters that Petrus Apponus reports Honorius of Thebes delivered. Chapter 30 ('Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists') says that among the Hebrews there are several fashions of characters, names three in one sentence (in J.F.'s English of 1651: the Celestial, 'because they shew it placed and figured amongst the Stars'; the Malachim, 'of Angels, or Regal'; and 'the passing through the River'), and shows them in a single woodcut: Celestial at the top, Malachim in the middle, Transitus fluvii at the bottom. The same chapter gives the nine-chamber cipher. Book II, chapter 22 gives the planetary squares with their seals and characters. In the 1533 Theban table the final sign carries a small ω.
letters.note: [S] celestial, malachim, theban, transitus-fluvii, aiq-bekar, planetary-seals, signs-of-the-art (Utrecht, Eton and Wellcome records; Peterson; the 1651 headings from EEBO-TCP and Peterson's transcription).
letters.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535)
letters.date: Book I was printed alone in 1531. The three books together: colophon 'Anno M.D.XXXIII. Mense Iulio' (July 1533). Catalogues report four or five issues dated 1533.
letters.place: [Cologne: Johannes Soter?]. Eton's catalogue queries the printer and records Adams's suggestion of Basel.
letters.locator: III.29; III.30; II.22; II.51. Page and signature in 1533 not verified.
letters.tookFrom: Theban: from Trithemius's Polygraphia (1518). Agrippa names Peter of Abano, not Trithemius; the dependence is shown by the agreement of the two texts, which Peterson's edition annotates. III.30: Agrippa presents the three alphabets as writings of the Hebrews 'delivered by Cabalists'. He does not name de Balmes (1523) or Panteo (1530), who had already printed the River script. letters.form: In 1887 William Wynn Westcott brought forward a set of ritual outlines written in English in a cipher alphabet taken from Trithemius, the Cipher Manuscripts, and in 1888 he, W. R. Woodman and S. L. MacGregor Mathers opened the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn on them. Westcott's account of a correspondence with a Fräulein Anna Sprengel, which authorised the Order, was judged by Ellic Howe (1972) and later R. A. Gilbert to be Westcott's own work. Its successor orders are living organisations: their papers and emblems are not reproduced here.

cautions: BASIS. This item was researched after the session's shared web-search budget had run out, and page fetching is not available. Each card is marked by its basis: [S] sibling research files written earlier in this session from web searches; [H] the site's own data; [P] prior knowledge, not verified in this run. Nothing marked [P] should be printed as fact until it has been checked. Postel (1538), Ambrosius (1539), Vigenère (1586), Rocca (1591), de Bry (1596) and Fry (1799) are whole-card [P]: show them with a 'to be checked' mark, or leave them out.
Every reprint re-cut the woodcuts (1550, 1561, 1651, Duret 1613, Barrett 1801). A drawing must name the edition it follows. Barrett's plate is third-hand from 1533.
Never write 'Honorius of Thebes invented the Theban' or 'Agrippa invented the Celestial'. Write 'Trithemius ascribes it to Honorius of Thebes' and 'Agrippa presents them as writings of the Hebrews'.
Do not date the Hebrew-keyed alphabets to 1510 (the draft) or to 1531 (Book I only). The first documented printing of III.29–30 is July 1533.
Do not call Agrippa Trithemius's pupil. The documented contact is the visit of 1509–10 and the letter of 8 April 1510.
The River script was printed in 1523 (de Balmes) and 1530 (Panteo) before Agrippa. Agrippa does not cite de Balmes; the pointer to de Balmes is Peterson's editorial note.
Postel's 1538 primer holds real alphabets, not magical ones, as far as this research knows. Do not present it as a grimoire.
Duret's place is Cologny, near Geneva, not Cologne (Peterson's slip).
The keys attached to the [P] cards (Vigenère, Duret's later alphabets) are leads, not findings: the comparison and alphabet pages must not cite these books for a letter form until a scan is checked.
Lévi: no table of the Agrippan alphabets is known to this research. Do not attribute the Alphabet of the Magi to Lévi. Paul Christian is only the leading candidate for its first printing.

Golden Dawn and its successor orders are living organisations. Do not reproduce their papers, rituals or emblems. Report the Sprengel letters as Westcott's account and the forgery as the conclusion of Howe and Gilbert. No source found shows Golden Dawn use of the Malachim or the Theban.
Sefer Raziel and the Jewish charm books belong to a living tradition. Describe them; neither mock nor endorse; report the Raziel story as legend.

Northern strand: List's Armanen row (1908) is modern and entered völkisch and National Socialist use; describe as history and do not reproduce SS emblems. Graves's tree-ogham (1948) is modern; report living practices neutrally.

Page numbers reported by cipher sites for the 1651 English (pp. 438–440) and the 1518 Polygraphia (p. 579 or 597) are unverified; Tory's folio (73r or 76v) is disputed.
